title: What Liquid actually is (and isn't)
excerpt: Liquid is Shopify's templating language - server-rendered, sandboxed, and everywhere in your theme. The 10-minute mental model.

blocks.p: Liquid is the language Shopify themes are written in. Every product page, cart and collection you see on a Shopify store is Liquid being rendered on Shopify's servers into plain HTML before it reaches the browser.

Liquid takes data (products, collections, customers, settings) and outputs HTML. It runs on Shopify's servers, not in the browser - there is no JavaScript framework, no build step, no npm install. You write a .liquid file, Shopify renders it, done.

list: Objects - {{ product.title }} prints a value. Objects are the data Shopify hands you: product, collection, cart, customer, shop, and hundreds more.
Tags - {% if %}, {% for %}, {% render %} control logic. They produce no visible output themselves.
Filters - {{ product.price | money }} transforms output. money formats currency, default provides fallbacks, image_url resizes images.

blocks.p: Read it aloud: if the product is available, print its title in capitals and its formatted price. Otherwise show a sold-out message. That is 90% of what Liquid does - conditionals around data.

list: Not JavaScript - it never runs in the browser; {% javascript %} blocks are the exception, and they run as plain JS after render.
Not a database language - you cannot query or write data. You read what Shopify gives you.
Not theme-agnostic magic - every theme organises its files differently; Dawn's structure is not Impulse's.
Not unlimited - Shopify enforces render-time and memory limits; deeply nested loops can fail.

blocks.p: Next lesson: where all this code actually lives inside a theme, and how to navigate the editor without getting lost.

title: Inside a Shopify theme: files, folders and render order
excerpt: layout/, templates/, sections/, snippets/ - what each folder does, which files load when, and how a page actually gets built.

blocks.p: Open any Shopify theme's code editor and you see a folder tree. It looks arbitrary until you know the four folders that matter - everything else is configuration.

list: layout/ - the skeleton. theme.liquid wraps every page: <head>, header, {{ content_for_layout }}, footer. One file for the whole store.
templates/ - one file per page type: product.json, collection.json, cart.json, index.json. JSON templates (OS 2.0) list which sections render and in what order.
sections/ - the building blocks. Each .liquid file here is a section the merchant can add, reorder or remove in the theme editor - IF it has a {% schema %} block.
snippets/ - reusable fragments rendered via {% render 'name' %}. No schema, no editor presence - pure code reuse.

blocks.h: How a product page gets built

blocks.p: 1. Shopify picks templates/product.json. 2. That JSON lists sections in order - typically main-product, then maybe featured-collection, then footer. 3. Each section's .liquid file renders with the product object available. 4. theme.liquid wraps the whole result with header and footer.

Online Store 2.0 themes (Dawn and everything built on it) use JSON templates - sections are data-driven and merchants reorder them visually. Vintage themes use .liquid templates with hardcoded {% section %} and {% include %} tags. Most modern work targets OS 2.0, but knowing both matters because client stores run both.

list: Product-page feature? sections/your-feature.liquid with a schema block - merchant adds it via editor.
Reusable piece used in 5 places? snippets/your-piece.liquid, rendered with {% render 'your-piece' %}.
Store-wide change (announcement bar, custom CSS)? theme.liquid or a section group in the header/footer.
One-off page? Use a custom template or a section with page-targeted presets.

blocks.p: The GPLMart library follows this exactly: every snippet ships as one self-contained file - paste it in snippets/ or sections/, and the install notes tell you which. Lesson three covers the syntax you'll actually write.

title: Liquid syntax crash course: objects, filters, tags
excerpt: The complete working vocabulary - every object type, the filters you'll use daily, and the tag patterns that cover 95% of theme code.

blocks.p: This is the reference lesson - the syntax table you'll come back to. Skim it now, use it as a cheat sheet later.
Double curly braces print a value. Always safe - Liquid escapes HTML by default.

list: money - price in cents to formatted currency: {{ 199900 | money }} → $1,999.00
default - fallback when nil/false: {{ product.metafields.custom.subtitle | default: product.title }}
date - format timestamps: {{ article.published_at | date: '%d %b %Y' }}
image_url - resize CDN images: {{ product.featured_image | image_url: width: 600 }}
strip_html / escape - clean text for meta tags and JSON-LD
handleize / handle - turn titles into URL-safe handles
json - serialize for JSON-LD and data attributes
where / reject - filter arrays: {{ product.images | where: 'attached_to_variant?', true }}

blocks.p: {% assign x = value %} sets a variable. {% capture x %}...{% endcapture %} grabs rendered output into a variable - essential for building strings.

list: {% render 'name', key: value %} - modern, isolated scope, pass data explicitly. Use this.
{% include 'name' %} - legacy, shares parent scope, deprecated in OS 2.0.
{% section 'name' %} - renders a section inside a template/section (legacy themes).
{% stylesheet %} / {% javascript %} - embed CSS/JS inside a single file. This is how every GPLMart one-file snippet works.

blocks.p: You now have the full vocabulary. Module 2 applies it to the most valuable page type in ecommerce: the product page.

title: The product object & metafields: your data layer
excerpt: Every field on product.* explained, plus metafields - the structured data layer that makes custom features possible.

blocks.p: The product object is the richest object in Liquid - 60+ fields. You don't need all of them; you need to know which exist and which are metafields.

list: product.title, product.handle, product.vendor, product.product_type
product.featured_image, product.images (array of image objects)
product.variants (array: id, title, price, compare_at_price, sku, available, featured_image)
product.options_with_values (variant option names + choices)
product.price, product.compare_at_price, product.price_varies
product.available, product.selected_or_first_available_variant
product.description, product.content (richer HTML description), product.tags
product.metafields.namespace.key - custom merchant data

blocks.p: Metafields are custom data fields merchants (or apps) attach to products, collections, customers, shops - anywhere. A 'fabric composition' or 'fit guide' that isn't a native Shopify field lives in a metafield. In Liquid: {{ product.metafields.custom.fabric }}. In JSON templates, section settings can expose metafields via the editor's dynamic sources.

blocks.h: A practical pattern: spec table from metafields

blocks.p: This renders nothing when the metafield is empty - the {% if %} guard means the section silently disappears instead of showing an empty table. That pattern (render only if data exists) is how you ship features that work across a whole catalogue without touching every product.

product.price shows the *selected or first available* variant's price - but on a product with variants, the displayed price must update when the customer picks a different variant. That's JavaScript territory (product JSON + fetch). For Liquid-only work, use product.selected_or_first_available_variant.price for server-rendered accuracy, and know that real variant switching needs the AJAX API - covered in the cart module.
Next: turning this data into the components that actually move conversion - buy boxes, stock indicators and trust elements.

title: The buy box: price, stock, variants and the add-to-cart that converts
excerpt: Why the buy box area decides 80% of product-page outcomes - and the exact Liquid patterns for each element.

blocks.p: The 'buy box' is the cluster around the add-to-cart button: price, compare-at, variant picker, stock indicator, trust badges, delivery estimate. It's where purchase intent either survives or dies.
Note the minus filter computing the real saving - never hardcode '20% off'; the data already knows the truth.

Fake scarcity ('only 2 left!' on a store with 500 units) is both dishonest and legally risky in some jurisdictions. The honest version reads real inventory levels - but Shopify's product.variants[].inventory_quantity is only exposed when the merchant tracks inventory AND the theme has permission. Pattern: show urgency only when inventory is genuinely low.

'Order in next 4 hours - delivery by Thursday' outperforms generic shipping text because it answers the real question (when will it arrive?). Calculate cutoff from shop.metaobjects or a metafield; render only if configured.

Payment icons, returns policy, guarantee strip - placed directly under the buy button where hesitation happens. Every GPLMart product-page snippet (trust-badges, payment-badges, guarantee-strip, delivery-estimator) is built for exactly this slot - preview them in the playground before writing your own.

list: Create sections/buy-box.liquid on a dev theme
Render price + compare-at + save amount
Add the inventory-aware stock line
Add a {% schema %} with settings for trust-badge text and cutoff hour
Test with a product that has variants AND one that doesn't

blocks.p: Module 3 takes you into the cart - where the AJAX API unlocks everything dynamic.
Member toolkit: listing copy directly affects buy-box conversion - the Product Listing Copy Skill writes titles, bullets and descriptions built for exactly this. See Products.

title: Variants, options and product customisation fields
excerpt: Variant pickers, option swatches, file uploads and personalization - the inputs that turn a product page into a configured order.

blocks.p: Variants are Shopify's answer to 'same product, different choices' - size, colour, material. The Liquid challenge: render pickers that update price, image and availability without a page reload.

list: product.options = ['Size', 'Colour'] - option names
product.options_with_values = [{name:'Size', values:['S','M','L']}, ...]
product.variants[] = every purchasable combination with its own price, sku, image, available flag
variant.featured_media / variant.image - per-variant imagery

blocks.h: The classic pattern: variant JSON + JS

blocks.p: Server-render all variants as JSON in a script tag; JavaScript listens to picker changes, finds the matching variant, and updates price/image/ATC button. Shopify's own themes do exactly this. Liquid provides the data; JS does the switching.

code.code:
<script type="application/json" data-variants>
[
{%- for v in product.variants -%}
  {
    "id": {{ v.id }},
    "title": {{ v.title | json }},
    "price": {{ v.price }},
    "available": {{ v.available }},
    "image": {{ v.featured_image | image_url: width: 800 | json }}
  }{%- unless forloop.last -%},{%- endunless -%}
{%- endfor -%}
]
</script>

blocks.p: Colour options deserve swatches (visual), size deserves buttons or a dropdown. The variant-swatches snippet in the library renders colour swatches from option values with hex mapping via metafields or a settings JSON. For text options, styled radio inputs beat native selects on mobile.

Engraving text, gift messages, file uploads - things that change per order but aren't purchasable variants - use line item properties. Inputs named properties[Engraving] inside the product form flow through to the order automatically. No app needed for basic text personalization.

code.code:
<input type="text" name="properties[Engraving text]" maxlength="40" placeholder="Name to engrave">
<textarea name="properties[Gift message]" rows="2"></textarea>

blocks.p: These show up in the order admin and confirmation email automatically. The personalization-field and file-upload snippets in the library implement this pattern with validation.
You've covered the product page's data and inputs. Module 3: what happens after add-to-cart.

title: The cart object and AJAX API: making the cart dynamic
excerpt: cart.* fields, /cart/add.js and /cart.js - the endpoints that power drawers, upsells and mini-carts without reloads.

blocks.p: The cart object (cart.item_count, cart.total_price, cart.items[]) renders server-side on cart pages. But modern storefronts need a live cart drawer that updates without navigation - that's the AJAX API.

list: GET /cart.js - returns the whole cart as JSON
POST /cart/add.js - adds an item {id, quantity, properties}
POST /cart/change.js - updates quantities
POST /cart/update.js - batch changes
POST /cart/clear.js - empties the cart
Render the drawer markup hidden in a section (cart-drawer snippet does this)
On add-to-cart success: fetch /cart.js, re-render item rows client-side or re-fetch a rendered snippet
Show free-shipping progress: (cart.total_price / threshold) - pure JS math on the JSON
Open the drawer with a CSS class toggle - no library needed

blocks.p: Post-add upsells use the same /cart/add.js call with a 'continue shopping' vs 'checkout' choice. Pre-purchase upsells (before ATC) are simpler - they're just links that add a different variant. The cart-upsell and upsell-modal snippets implement both patterns.

list: Checkout itself (checkout page) is NOT customizable via Liquid on standard plans - Shopify checkout extensibility is a separate system.
Cart page IS a JSON template - you can rebuild it entirely.
Always handle the error response - /cart/add.js returns 422 with description when a variant is unavailable.
Debounce rapid clicks; double-adds are the #1 AJAX cart bug.

blocks.p: Module 4: making all of this controllable by merchants through the theme editor.

title: Create your Shopify account and pick the right plan
excerpt: From signup to a live store shell - which plan to choose, domain basics, and the settings to fix on day one.

blocks.p: Everything starts at shopify.com. You'll create an account, answer a few onboarding questions, and land inside the admin - the control room for your entire store.

list: Go to shopify.com and click 'Start for free' - every plan gets a 3-day trial (sometimes extended offers appear).
Enter your email, create a password, and name your store. The store name becomes your myshopify.com subdomain - pick something short and brandable; you can connect a real domain later.
Answer the onboarding questions honestly (what you sell, where) - they only affect suggested apps, nothing is locked in.

img.caption: The admin home - your store's mission control. Everything below lives in this sidebar.

blocks.h: Step 2 - Pick a plan (this decision matters)

list: Basic (~₹2,000/mo or ~$39): right for 95% of new stores. Full theme editing, reports, discount codes - everything you need.
Shopify (~₹7,500/mo): only when you outgrow Basic's staff accounts or need professional reports.
Advanced/Plus: for high-volume stores - ignore these for now.

blocks.p: Honest advice: start on Basic. Upgrading later takes 2 minutes and doesn't break anything - downgrading mid-month does, so don't buy Advanced 'just in case'.

list: Settings > General: store name, sender email, store currency, timezone, units.
Settings > Locations: add your real business address - required for payments and shipping anyway.
Settings > Markets (or International): decide India-only first, expand later - simpler shipping and taxes.
Settings > Policies: generate the refund/privacy/terms templates Shopify provides, then edit them to match your store.

blocks.p: Next lesson: installing a theme and making it look like YOUR brand, not a template.

title: Install a theme and make it yours
excerpt: Free vs paid themes, theme editor basics, brand colours/fonts, and the 5 changes that make a store look professional.

blocks.p: Your theme is the skeleton of the store - everything customers see is controlled by it. Choose well once; switching themes later means rebuilding pages.

list: Free themes (Dawn is the default and genuinely good): fast, OS 2.0, section-based, zero cost. Start here.
Paid themes ($180-400 one-time on Theme Store): more built-in sections and presets. Worth it only if a specific feature saves you building it.
Avoid 'nulled' or shared premium themes from random sites - they contain malware and violate licenses. This is non-negotiable.
Online Store > Themes > Add theme > 'Visit Theme Store' - install Dawn (free) or your pick.
Click 'Customize' to open the theme editor - the left panel lists every section, the right shows live preview.
Brand basics: Theme settings > Colors (pick 2-3 brand colours), Typography (1-2 fonts max), Favicon (your logo mark).

blocks.h: The 5 changes that make it look professional

list: Announcement bar: one line - free shipping threshold or a offer. Online Store > Themes > Customize > Announcement bar.
Logo + brand colours everywhere - inconsistent branding is the #1 'cheap store' tell.
Real product photos - never supplier stock images alone; even a clean phone photo beats a generic one.
Footer: real contact info, policy links, social icons. Empty footers scream unfinished.
Remove demo content: Dawn ships with placeholder products/images - delete or replace ALL of it before launch.

blocks.p: Rule of thumb: a store with 5 real products and honest content beats a store with 500 demo items. Next: menus and homepage.

title: Menus, homepage & the pages that build trust
excerpt: Header/footer navigation, a homepage that converts, and the About/Contact/Policy pages customers check before buying.

blocks.p: Navigation decides whether shoppers find products; the homepage decides whether they stay. Both take 30 minutes and most stores get them wrong.

img.alt: Header and footer menu structure diagram
img.caption: Keep the header to 4-6 items max. Dropdowns for collections, not everything flat.

list: Main menu: Home, Shop (dropdown: collections), maybe Sale or New. That's it - 4-6 items.
Footer menu: Shop, Help (Shipping/Returns/FAQ), Company (About/Contact), Legal (Privacy/Terms/Refund).
Never link to pages that don't exist yet - a 404 in the menu kills trust instantly.
Hero: one clear promise + one CTA button ('Shop now'), real product image - not a slider of 5 banners.
Featured collection: your bestsellers or hero products, 4-8 items.
Trust strip: shipping time, returns policy, payment icons, rating - the answers to 'is this legit?'.
Social proof: testimonials or review quotes once you have them.
Newsletter signup with a reason to join ('10% off first order').

blocks.h: The trust pages nobody reads until they do

list: About: who you are, why the store exists - 2 short paragraphs + a real photo.
Contact: email + WhatsApp number + address. A store with no contact page is an automatic refund-risk flag.
Shipping/Returns/FAQ: concrete answers - 'delivery in 5-12 days', '7-day returns', not vague promises.

blocks.p: These pages are also where the GPLMart snippets shine - FAQ accordion, trust grid, announcement bar are all one-file installs. Next: products and pricing.

title: Add products properly: variants, pricing and collections
excerpt: The product form field-by-field, pricing psychology that protects margin, and collections that sell.

blocks.p: Products → Add product is where stores are won or lost. A sloppy product page converts at half the rate of a clean one.

blocks.h: The product form, field by field

list: Title: specific, not clever - 'Men's Cotton Oversized T-Shirt - Black' beats 'Awesome Tee'.
Description: features AND benefits, scannable bullets, sizing/fit info, what's in the box. ~150-300 words.
Media: 3-7 images minimum - front, back, detail, size chart, lifestyle. Video helps if you have it.
Pricing: enter cost-per-item mentally - price must cover product + shipping + fees + profit (next lesson covers the math).
Variants: Size/Colour options under 'Options' - Shopify generates every combination automatically.
Organization: product type, vendor, tags, and WHICH collections it belongs to.
Charm pricing works (₹499 vs ₹500) but don't overdo it - round numbers signal quality for premium goods.
Compare-at price must be a REAL former price - fake 'was ₹999' prices violate consumer law in India (and Meta ad policies).
Bundle math: '3 for ₹1,299' lifts AOV better than 10% off - the bundle-save and quantity-breaks snippets automate this.
Free shipping threshold: set it ~20% above your average order so it pulls carts over the line (free-shipping-bar snippet shows progress).
Manual collections for curated drops ('New arrivals', 'Best sellers').
Smart collections for rules ('price < ₹999 AND tag:summer').
Name collections like customers search: ' Men's Kurtas' not 'Collection 3'.

blocks.p: Inventory tip: for dropshipping you don't stock anything - set inventory tracking OFF or use 'continue selling when out of stock' until you understand supplier lead times.

Member toolkit: the Product Listing Copy Skill turns these pricing and product decisions into ready-to-paste titles, bullets and descriptions - see Products > Product Listing Copy Skill, plus the Product Listing Copy Bible ebook.

title: Payments: Razorpay, Stripe and COD for India + international
excerpt: Activate the payment methods your buyers actually use - UPI/COD for India, cards for the world.

blocks.p: Payment setup is where new stores lose sales silently - a checkout that doesn't offer the buyer's preferred method is an abandoned cart.

list: Razorpay: Settings > Payments > Razorpay - KYC (PAN, bank details, business proof) takes 2-5 days. Supports UPI, cards, netbanking, wallets.
Cash on Delivery: enable under COD settings - COD still drives 40-60% of Indian ecommerce orders. Set a COD fee or minimum order to cover RTO risk.
RTO (return-to-origin) is the COD killer: orders never delivered cost you shipping both ways. Mitigate with partial advance payment or phone verification apps.
Stripe: activate via Shopify Payments where available, or the Stripe app - needs business docs; supports 135+ currencies and cards globally.
PayPal: the trust signal international buyers look for - especially for unknown brands.
Shopify Payments isn't available in India directly - Razorpay is the standard Indian gateway; international sellers often run Razorpay (India entity) + Stripe (foreign entity) together.

blocks.p: Place a real test order on your own store with a small amount. Check: order confirmation email, admin order view, payment capture, and that the customer gets tracking later. An untested payment flow is a launch blocker.
Next lesson: connecting CJdropshipping and the full order-fulfilment flow.

title: CJdropshipping: sourcing and fulfilment without inventory
excerpt: Connect CJ to Shopify, import products, and the exact flow an order takes from your store to the customer's door.

blocks.p: Dropshipping = you sell, the supplier ships. You never hold stock - which means zero inventory risk, but also zero quality control. Supplier choice IS your business.

img.caption: Four steps - the customer never knows (or cares) you didn't ship it.

list: Create a CJdropshipping account (free) - verify email, complete basic profile.
Install the CJdropshipping app from the Shopify App Store and connect your store.
Browse products: filter by category, shipping country, and 'US warehouse'/'India warehouse' stock for faster delivery.
Import with 'List to Shopify' - CJ auto-maps title, images, variants and pricing. Then EDIT everything: rewrite descriptions, replace images, fix pricing.
Set your shipping rates in Shopify (Settings > Shipping) to roughly match CJ's shipping cost + margin.
Order appears in Shopify admin AND syncs to CJ automatically (if auto-fulfilment is on).
CJ ships direct to customer with YOUR store name on the packing slip option (enable branded invoicing in CJ settings - critical for trust).
Tracking number syncs back to Shopify and emails the customer automatically.
Shipping times: India 5-12 days, US/EU 10-25 days - your product pages MUST state this or you drown in 'where is my order' tickets.
Quality varies - order samples of anything you'll scale ($5-15 well spent).
Don't sell branded/trademarked items (Nike, Disney etc) - legal trouble, not a grey area.
Alternatives worth knowing: AliExpress Dropshipping, Zendrop, Spocket (US/EU focus, faster shipping, higher cost).

blocks.p: Next module: finding products people actually want to buy - before you import a single one.

Member toolkit: once you pick winning products, the Product Photoshoot Skill turns supplier images into clean listing photos - and the Product Listing Copy Skill writes the listing itself. See Products.

title: Meta setup: Business Manager, pixel and the tracking that matters
excerpt: Business portfolio, ad account, pixel installation and verifying that Purchase events actually fire.

blocks.p: Every rupee of ad spend is wasted if tracking is broken. This lesson is unglamorous and non-negotiable - do it before writing a single ad.

list: business.facebook.com → create a Business Portfolio (one per business, not per ad account).
Add your ad account inside it - start with one account; don't fragment budgets early.
Add a payment method and complete account verification - unverified accounts get restricted fast.
Shopify makes this easy: Settings > Customer events > 'Add custom pixel' OR use the official Facebook & Instagram sales channel which auto-installs it.
Verify in Events Manager → Test events: browse your store, add to cart, and watch PageView/AddToCart/Purchase events fire in real time.
Enable 'Automatic advanced matching' - it improves attribution significantly.
Meta catalog = your product feed for dynamic ads and shopping placements.
Connect via the Facebook channel or feed URL - Shopify generates it automatically.
Check catalog diagnostics weekly - disapproved items (policy violations, missing prices) silently kill ad delivery.
CTR (click-through rate): below 1% = weak creative or wrong audience.
CPC / CPM: your traffic cost - compare against product margin, not vanity benchmarks.
ROAS: revenue ÷ ad spend. Break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ your margin (40% margin → need 2.5x just to break even).
CPA: cost per purchase - the number that decides if ads are profitable.

blocks.p: Tracking done right = every later lesson works. Next: campaign structure that scales without chaos.

title: Professional theme customisation: build a brand system, not a template
excerpt: Theme settings deep-dive - colours, typography, spacing and the reusable patterns that make a store look designed, not assembled.

blocks.p: A store that looks 'template-y' loses trust before the first product click. The fix isn't a fancier theme - it's a consistent system: 2-3 colours, 1-2 fonts, consistent spacing, and the same visual language on every page.
Decide these once, write them down, and never deviate:

list: Primary colour: buttons, links, accents (one bold colour).
Secondary colour: badges, sale tags, secondary buttons.
Neutral background + text colours: usually near-white bg, near-black text.
Font pairing: one display font for headings, one body font for everything else. Google Fonts is fine.

blocks.h: Step 2 - Apply them in Theme settings

list: Online Store > Themes > Customize > Theme settings > Colors: set every colour role - background, foreground, primary button, secondary button, sale price, sale badge.
Typography: heading font + body font, then set heading weight/letter-spacing. Bigger headings with tighter spacing look premium.
Product cards: set card style (border vs shadow), image ratio (square or portrait consistently), and badge positions.

img.caption: Theme editor lives under Online Store > Themes > Customize - every change previews live on the right.

blocks.h: Step 3 - The details that signal 'real store'

list: Announcement bar: rotate 2-3 short messages (free shipping, new drop, sale) - set rotation in the section settings.
Product image consistency: same background colour, same angle style, same crop ratio across the catalogue. Mixed photos scream marketplace, not brand.
Whitespace: resist filling every section. Premium stores breathe - one strong section beats three crowded ones.
Favicon + social share image: Settings for favicon; upload a branded OG image so shared links look professional.

blocks.p: Rule: if a customer can't tell your store apart from a generic template in 5 seconds, the design isn't done. Next lesson: catalogue operations at scale.

title: Catalogue & fulfilment operations: run the store like a system
excerpt: Bulk editing, inventory locations, fulfilment workflows and the operational habits that prevent stock disasters.

blocks.p: Operations is where growing stores break. The goal: systems that keep stock, orders and fulfilment accurate without daily manual heroics.

list: Weekly 15-minute audit: Products > All products > filter 'No collection' and 'No image' - fix or delete.
Bulk editor (Products > Select products > Bulk edit): change prices, tags, collections across hundreds of SKUs at once. Learn it once, save hours weekly.
Duplicate products before seasonal relaunches - never edit last year's product that has order history.
Tags are your search/filter power: use a consistent scheme (color:black, material:cotton, season:summer) - spaces not hyphens.
Settings > Locations: one location per physical stock point. Multi-location only if you actually ship from multiple places.
Inventory tracking ON for products you stock; for dropshipped items decide per supplier - tracking OFF avoids oversell confusion, but watch supplier stock.
Set 'continue selling when out of stock' OFF unless you can fulfil backorders - overselling kills reviews.
Low-stock alerts: Shopify doesn't email you natively - use the free Stocky app or a simple scheduled check.
Orders > Unfulfilled: process daily, not weekly - fast dispatch = fewer cancellations and better reviews.
Print packing slips in batches; group orders by shipping method.
Mark fulfilled ONLY after the courier scans - premature 'fulfilled' emails lie to customers.
Returns: decide policy upfront (7-day? who pays return shipping?), write it on the policy page, and honour it consistently.

blocks.p: Operations done right is invisible - customers just get their orders on time, every time. Next: marketing and conversion.

title: Email & WhatsApp marketing: the owned channels that convert
excerpt: Build your list, send campaigns that sell, and use WhatsApp broadcasts - the highest-ROI marketing for Indian stores.

blocks.p: Ads rent attention; email and WhatsApp own it. For Indian ecommerce especially, WhatsApp campaigns routinely outperform email on open rates.

list: Every signup needs a reason: '10% off first order', 'early access to drops', 'restock alerts'. No reason = no emails.
Place the signup form site-wide (footer + popup on exit-intent or after 30s) - but ONE popup, not three stacked.
Import existing customers from Orders (Customers > Export CSV) - they've already bought, they're your warmest list.
Welcome series (3 emails): discount code → bestsellers → social proof. Set-and-forget revenue.
Abandoned cart: Shopify Emails or Klaviyo free tier sends automatically - recover 5-15% of lost carts.
Weekly campaign formula: one product/story + one clear CTA. Subject lines under 50 chars, preview text that adds info not repeats.
Segment: send sale alerts only to buyers, new-arrival alerts to everyone - irrelevant emails train people to unsubscribe.
Broadcast lists (up to 256 contacts per list) via WhatsApp Business app - free to start.
Use it for: order updates, restock alerts, festival sale announcements, COD order confirmations.
Rules: get opt-in first (checkout checkbox 'Order updates on WhatsApp'), keep messages short, always identify the store.
Never blast promotions to people who didn't opt in - WhatsApp bans for spam and you lose the channel.

blocks.p: Measure: email revenue and WhatsApp reply rates weekly. If a channel isn't driving sales in 30 days, fix the offer before blaming the channel.

Member toolkit: the Email & WhatsApp Copy Skill provides ready sequence templates (welcome, cart recovery, win-back) plus the WhatsApp Marketing Playbook ebook for the India-specific rules. See Products.

title: Analytics, margins & scaling: grow without breaking profit
excerpt: Read your numbers correctly, protect margin at scale, and know the real signals that you're ready to spend on ads.

blocks.p: Most stores don't fail from lack of traffic - they fail from not knowing their numbers. This lesson is the financial dashboard every owner needs.

list: Revenue: total sales - but meaningless without context.
AOV (average order value): revenue ÷ orders. Bundles and free-shipping thresholds exist to lift this.
Gross margin: (price - product cost - shipping cost) ÷ price. Know it per product, not as an average.
CAC (customer acquisition cost): ad spend ÷ new customers. Only meaningful once you run paid.
Repeat rate: % of customers who buy again. Above 20-25% = healthy; below 10% = fix retention first.
Razorpay/Stripe fees (~2% + GST) and shipping subsidies eat margin silently - recalculate pricing quarterly.
Returns/RTO are a margin line item, not an ops issue: COD stores often lose 15-25% to RTO. Track it monthly.
Price increases: test on new customers first (they don't know the old price). Loyal customers forgive 5-10% rises if quality held.
Never discount below margin floor - a 'sale' that loses money per order is just subsidised growth.
Checklist: 20+ orders, know your margin per product, email/WhatsApp flows live, tracking verified, return policy honoured consistently.
Start small: ₹500-1000/day test budget, one campaign, one audience - enough data in 3-5 days to judge.
Scale only winners: double budget on campaigns with ROAS above break-even for 5+ consecutive days, not on day-one spikes.

blocks.p: The Facebook Ads course takes over from here - but only after these foundations are solid. Scaling broken unit economics with ads just loses money faster.
Member toolkit: the SEO Audit Skill runs a structured store audit - technical, on-page, content gaps and a 30/60/90 fix roadmap. See Products.

title: {% schema %} and theme editor settings: make merchants love your sections
excerpt: The JSON schema block that turns a hardcoded section into a customisable, editor-friendly component.

blocks.p: A section without {% schema %} is invisible to the theme editor - merchants can't add, configure or reorder it. Schema is what separates 'code snippet' from 'professional theme component'.
Every setting becomes section.settings.<id>: {{ section.settings.text }}, and colour settings work directly in style attributes. Toggle/checkbox returns true/false for {% if %} checks.

list: text / textarea / richtext - strings; richtext allows basic HTML
color - hex picker; pair with background/style usage
checkbox - boolean toggles
range - number slider (min/max/step/unit)
select - dropdown from options array
url - link picker (pages, products, collections, or external)
image_picker - media library image
font_picker / color_background - theme-editor native pickers
header - visual group divider in the editor panel
paragraph - plain-text instructions inside the editor
presets: [{name}] - what appears when merchant clicks 'Add section'. Multiple presets = multiple pre-configured variants.
blocks: [...] inside schema - repeatable inner items (slides, features, testimonials). Merchants add/remove/reorder them in the editor.
max_blocks - cap how many blocks a section accepts.

blocks.p: Design rule: every setting needs a sensible default so the section looks right before the merchant touches anything. Test by adding the section to a fresh page with zero configuration.

title: Performance: render cost, caching and keeping custom code fast
excerpt: Why custom Liquid slows stores down, how to measure it, and the patterns that keep snippets cheap at scale.

blocks.p: Shopify renders every page server-side with strict time and memory budgets. A snippet that's fast on your dev store can time out on a 10,000-product catalogue. Performance isn't optional polish - it's correctness.

list: Nested loops: {% for product in collection.products %} inside another {% for %} multiplies work fast - paginate or limit.
Repeated object access: {{ product.metafields... }} called 10 times re-evaluates - {% assign %} once, reuse.
Huge arrays: all_products, collection.products without limit render EVERYTHING - always paginate or slice.
External requests: image_url with extreme sizes, many render calls per page - each adds latency.
JavaScript weight: big {% javascript %} blocks parse on every page - keep under ~10KB per snippet.
limit + offset: {{ collection.products | limit: 12 }} never renders more than needed.
assign once: {% assign img = product.featured_image | image_url: width: 600 %} then reuse {{ img }}.
lazy-render below fold: wrap heavy sections in details/summary or render on interaction.
Cache-friendly markup: avoid random values in class names that bust CDN caching.
image_url sizing: request the size you'll display, not the original - width: 600 not width: 2000.
Theme editor > ... > 'View render time' isn't exposed - use Shopify's built-in 'Theme check' plus Lighthouse on the storefront.
Lighthouse mobile: aim LCP < 2.5s, TBT < 200ms - custom snippets should add < 50ms.
If a page slows after adding a snippet, binary-search: disable sections one at a time to isolate.

blocks.p: Rule of thumb: if your snippet needs a nested loop over products AND collections, it's probably doing too much - split it into two smaller snippets.

title: Search, filters & localization: the store features merchants ask for
excerpt: Customise search results, collection filtering and multi-currency/multi-language without apps.

blocks.p: Search and filtering directly affect whether shoppers find products. Shopify's defaults work but are generic - here's how to make them actually good.

list: Search results page uses search.results / search.filters - check which template your theme uses (main-search.liquid).
Improve relevance: ensure product titles/descriptions/tags contain the words customers actually type - SEO and search share vocabulary.
Empty state matters: 'No results for X' should suggest collections or bestsellers, not dead-end.
Predictive search (OS 2.0 themes have it built-in) uses the /search/suggest.json endpoint - ensure product data is complete for it to shine.
OS 2.0 themes have filter groups in the editor - enable price, availability, and up to 2 custom filter sources.
Custom filters need metafields: create a 'filterable' metafield definition, tag products, then enable it in the collection section's filter settings.
Sort options: price low-high, newest, best-selling - enable only the ones your catalogue supports meaningfully.
Filter UX rule: show result count live updating; hide empty filter values rather than letting users pick nothing.
Markets (Settings > Markets): sell in multiple countries/currencies - Shopify handles currency conversion and domain/subfolder structure.
request.locale / localization.country in Liquid - show country-appropriate content (shipping promises, phone formats).
Translations: Themes > Edit languages - translate theme text without touching code; product content needs separate translation apps or manual entry.
Don't over-engineer: India-only store = single market, INR, en-IN. Add markets when you actually sell internationally.

blocks.p: These features feel 'app-like' but they're theme-level - no monthly fees, no script bloat. That's the GPLMart advantage.

title: Shipping client work: scope, quote, deliver and get paid
excerpt: The business side of Liquid freelancing - what to charge, how to scope, and how to deliver work clients actually pay for.

blocks.p: Liquid skills are worthless without a delivery process. This lesson is the playbook for turning snippet knowledge into invoiceable work.

list: Not 'Liquid code' - outcomes: 'product page that converts better', 'cart that recovers abandoned sales', 'store that looks premium'.
Clients pay for certainty: fixed scope, clear deliverables, a date. Hourly billing invites scope creep arguments.
Your unfair advantage: a tested snippet library. 'I already have a battle-tested solution for this' justifies premium pricing.
Discovery questions: theme name/version, OS 2.0 or vintage, existing customisations, deadline, budget range.
Always ask for admin/staff access OR a copy of the theme - never work blind on live stores.
Deliverable definition: '3 custom sections + installation + 1 revision round + 7-day bugfix window' beats 'customise my store'.
Red flags: 'just quickly change this', no access, expecting apps-level features in pure Liquid, budget under your floor.
Single snippet customisation: ₹1,500-5,000 depending on complexity.
Custom section build from scratch: ₹8,000-25,000.
Full product-page or cart rebuild: ₹30,000-80,000.
Retainer for ongoing tweaks: ₹10,000-25,000/month for 2-3 small changes/month.
Charge 50% upfront, 50% on delivery - non-negotiable for new clients.
Test on a development theme/store first - never edit live directly.
Document what you changed: which files, which settings, how to revert.
Hand over clean code with comments - clients who can read it trust you more and pay faster.
Follow up at day 7: 'everything working? anything need adjusting?' - prevents refund requests and earns referrals.

blocks.p: Your own GPLMart library is also a portfolio - 'here's my production snippet library' sells better than any profile page.

title: Find winning products for the Indian market (without guessing)
excerpt: Validated research methods - trending searches, margin math after shipping, and how to spot products Indian buyers will actually pay for.

blocks.p: The #1 reason Indian dropshipping stores fail: they import random 'trending' products with no Indian demand. Winning product research is a system, not luck.

blocks.h: Where to look for demand signals

list: Google Trends (India): rising searches = rising demand. Filter 'Past 12 months' to spot sustained trends vs one-day spikes.
Amazon India bestsellers + Flipkart trends: what's already selling proves demand - you're looking for better-priced supply, not new categories.
Instagram Reels/YouTube Shorts: products going viral in Indian content (kitchen gadgets, phone accessories, fitness, car accessories) - early signal before it peaks.
Meesho/GlowRoad trending: what Indian resellers already push successfully - validated demand, thin margins though.

blocks.h: The margin math that kills most picks

blocks.p: A product isn't winning until the math works. For a ₹799 sell price:

list: Product cost from supplier: ₹250-400
Shipping to customer (India): ₹60-120
Payment gateway fee (Razorpay ~2%): ~₹16
Platform/ads cost per order: ₹50-150 (once you advertise)
Realistic margin: ₹150-300 per order = 20-35% - thin but workable at volume

blocks.p: Products under ₹499 sell on volume but razor-thin margins; ₹999-1999 hits the sweet spot - high enough margin, impulse-buyable price.

blocks.h: Red flags that mean 'skip this product'

list: Fragile/glass items - Indian shipping breaks them, returns kill you.
Electronics with batteries - shipping restrictions + warranty nightmares.
Anything branded/trademarked - legal risk, not worth it.
Products needing size/fit certainty (clothing without size charts) - return rates explode.
Oversized/heavy items - shipping eats the margin entirely.

blocks.p: Validate before importing: check 3-5 competitors' prices, read their reviews for complaints (those are your opportunities), and order a sample if the margin justifies it.
Member toolkit: validate product photos with the Product Photoshoot Skill and write listings with the Product Listing Copy Skill before spending on ads. See Products.

title: Cash on Delivery & RTO: the India-specific profit killer
excerpt: COD drives orders but return-to-origin destroys margins - the exact rules and tools to keep COD profitable.

blocks.p: Cash on Delivery is non-negotiable in India - 40-60% of orders are COD. But every undelivered COD order costs you product + shipping both ways. RTO management is the difference between profit and loss.

list: Fake orders: bots and prank orders with random phone numbers - biggest RTO source.
Changed mind: customer orders impulsively, refuses at door.
Address problems: incomplete addresses, remote areas, wrong phone numbers.
Courier failures: multiple delivery attempts missed.
Phone verification: require OTP verification on the phone number at checkout - kills fake orders instantly. Shopify apps like 'OTP Verification' do this.
Partial advance payment: even ₹50-99 advance filters fake orders massively while keeping COD available.
COD limits by pin code: disable COD for high-RTO areas (remote/jhuggi zones) - delivery partners share RTO data.
Address quality: require landmark field, disable COD on PO boxes/incomplete addresses.
Order velocity check: flag orders >3x your average daily volume - often bot attacks.
COD fee: charge ₹30-50 handling fee or bake into price - never offer free COD, it attracts the worst customers.
Minimum order value for COD: ₹299-499 filters tiny orders where fees exceed margin.
Razorpay/PayU both support COD with configurable rules - check Settings > Payments > COD options.

blocks.p: Track RTO rate weekly: (returned COD orders ÷ total COD orders). Under 15% = healthy; 15-25% = fix something; above 25% = stop COD on those products/pincodes immediately.

title: Marketing to Indian buyers: WhatsApp, Instagram and regional reach
excerpt: The channels that actually work in India - WhatsApp broadcasts, Instagram Reels, regional content and festive-season spikes.

blocks.p: Indian ecommerce marketing is different: WhatsApp beats email, vernacular content outperforms English, and festival calendars drive 40% of annual sales.

list: Opt-in at checkout: 'Get order updates + exclusive deals on WhatsApp' checkbox - builds your list automatically.
Broadcast strategy: weekly catalogue drops, festival announcements, back-in-stock alerts. Keep it to 1-2 messages/week max.
WhatsApp Business app (free): labels for customers, quick replies, catalog feature built-in.
Click-to-WhatsApp ads: Facebook/Instagram ads that open a chat - highest intent traffic in India right now.
Reels > static posts: 15-30 second product demos, before/after, unboxing - Indian audiences discover products here first.
Regional languages: Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Bengali content massively outperforms English-only for non-metro audiences.
Collabs > ads early: micro-influencers (10k-100k followers) in your niche charge ₹2k-15k per post - better ROI than cold ads for new stores.
Big sale windows: Republic Day, Holi, Eid, Raksha Bandhan, Diwali (Oct-Nov = biggest), New Year, Republic Day sales.
Start preparing 3-4 weeks before: stock check, creatives ready, WhatsApp broadcast drafted, ad budget set.
COD demand spikes during festivals - ensure your RTO rules are tightened before big sale days.

blocks.p: Reality check: organic reach is limited - plan to spend ₹500-2000/day on Meta ads once product-market fit is proven. Marketing amplifies a working store; it doesn't fix a broken one.

Member toolkit: the Email & WhatsApp Copy Skill has WhatsApp broadcast templates and the WhatsApp Marketing Playbook ebook covers opt-in, the 24-hour rule and broadcast structures. The Shopify Launch Video Skill makes announcement reels. See Products.

title: Global product research: find winners for US & EU markets
excerpt: Trend tools, ad-spy research and margin validation for international dropshipping - data over guessing.

blocks.p: International dropshipping rewards research discipline - US/EU markets are more competitive but pay 3-5x the margins of India. The tools exist; most people skip them.

blocks.h: The research stack (free tier is enough)

list: Google Trends (US/EU): rising queries in your target market - filter by country, compare regions.
TikTok Creative Center: trending products and top ads by country - the fastest product discovery tool right now.
Facebook Ad Library: search competitor ads in your niche - what's being advertised heavily = proven demand.
Amazon Movers & Shakers / Best Sellers: products gaining rank fast = emerging demand.
CJdropshipping 'Hot products' + Zendrop curated lists: supplier-validated winners.
Search the product on Amazon US - if it's already a bestseller at $30, you can't compete on price; find a differentiated angle (bundle, colour, niche use-case).
Check shipping cost + delivery time from your supplier BEFORE calculating margin - slow shipping kills conversion.
Read 20+ reviews of competitor products - complaints are your product improvement opportunity.
Seasonality: use Google Trends 5-year view - avoid products that only spike one month unless you plan around it.
Sell price: $39.99 (psychological price point)
Product cost: $8-12
Shipping (ePacket/CJPacket): $3-6
Payment processing (~3%): ~$1.20
Ad cost per order (target): $10-15
Net margin target: $10-18 per order = 25-45% - healthy for scaling

blocks.p: Rule: if you can't hit 25% net margin AFTER ads, the product doesn't work - no amount of creative fixes bad unit economics.

Member toolkit: the Product Listing Copy Skill adapts listings per marketplace (Amazon vs Shopify vs eBay), and the Product Photoshoot Skill creates clean product images from supplier shots. See Products.

title: International suppliers & shipping: CJ, Zendrop, AliExpress compared
excerpt: Choose the right supplier for US/EU fulfilment - shipping times, costs, quality and the honest trade-offs of each.

blocks.p: Supplier choice determines your shipping time, cost and product quality - the three things international customers judge you on. Get this wrong and nothing else matters.

list: CJdropshipping: largest catalogue, own warehouses (US/EU/Asia), 7-15 day US shipping, ~$0.5-2/order platform fee. Best all-rounder for beginners.
Zendrop: curated US-based suppliers, 3-7 day US shipping, higher product cost but faster + better quality control. Best for brand-building.
AliExpress Dropshipping: cheapest product costs, 10-20 day shipping, inconsistent quality, highest RTO/dispute risk. Only for ultra-price-sensitive niches.
Spocket: US/EU suppliers only, 2-5 day shipping, premium pricing - best for high-AOV stores where speed matters.

blocks.h: How to evaluate a specific product

list: Check actual shipping time TO your target country - '7-15 days' means to China warehouse; US warehouse stock ships faster.
Calculate landed cost: product + shipping + any platform fee + payment processing - that's your true cost.
Order a sample: $5-15 well spent. Check packaging quality, product accuracy vs photos, and whether it arrives undamaged.
Read supplier reviews on the platform - look for 'late shipping' and 'wrong item' complaints specifically.

blocks.h: Setting delivery expectations on your store

list: Product pages MUST state: 'Ships from [country], delivery in X-Y business days'. Vague shipping = chargebacks.
Order confirmation email: set clear timeline ('ships within 24-48h, delivery 7-12 days').
Tracking: CJ/Zendrop auto-sync tracking to Shopify - customer gets updates automatically.
Pro tip: say 'estimated delivery' not 'guaranteed' - protects you legally while staying honest.

blocks.p: Start with CJdropshipping for catalogue breadth; move bestsellers to Zendrop/Spocket for faster shipping once revenue justifies it.

title: International payments: Stripe, PayPal and multi-currency done right
excerpt: Accept cards globally, handle currencies correctly, and avoid the tax/duty mistakes that kill international stores.

blocks.p: International customers expect card checkout, PayPal option, and prices in their currency. Get payments wrong and cart abandonment spikes to 70%+.

list: Stripe: primary card processor - 135+ currencies, ~2.9% + $0.30 per transaction, fraud protection built-in. Activate via Shopify Payments or Stripe app.
PayPal: the trust signal - many US/EU buyers won't buy without it. ~3.49% + fixed fee. Worth the slightly higher fee for conversion.
Shopify Payments (where available): native integration, fastest checkout, lower fees than third-party. Check availability for your entity country.
Markets feature: create separate markets for US, EU, UK - each with own currency, pricing, and optionally domain.
Price in local currency, not 'USD converted': round prices psychologically ($49.99 not $52.37).
Shopify Payments auto-converts; third-party gateways need Markets + manual price adjustments.
Don't show all currencies to everyone - confuse buyers, kill conversion. One market = one currency.
US: most states charge sales tax - Shopify can auto-collect via Tax settings or apps like TaxJar. Don't ignore it.
EU/UK: VAT/GST rules are complex - use Shopify's tax settings or hire an accountant for EU sales.
Duties/customs: decide DDP (delivered duty paid - you cover it, higher price) vs DDU (buyer pays at door - cheaper for you, surprise costs for them). DDP converts better.
Start US-only if possible: single tax regime, English market, largest dropshipping market.

blocks.p: Test checkout in every currency before launch - currency conversion bugs are silent killers.

title: Cross-border marketing: run profitable Meta ads for US/EU
excerpt: Campaign structure, creative localisation and budget pacing for international ecommerce - where most dropshippers lose money.

blocks.p: International dropshipping lives or dies on paid ads - organic won't cut it in competitive US/EU markets. The Facebook Ads course covers Meta deeply; this lesson focuses on what's different for cross-border.

list: Start US-only: largest market, English creatives, single timezone for testing. Expand to EU/UK after US is profitable.
Advantage+ Shopping campaigns (ASC): Meta's AI-driven campaign type - simplest for beginners, decent results for ecommerce.
Manual campaigns once scaling: separate ad sets per audience/angle, clearer testing.
Budget pacing: start $20-50/day per campaign - enough data in 3-5 days without burning cash.
UGC-style ads outperform polished ads: phone-shot videos, 'I tried this' hooks, before/after - feels authentic not advertised.
First 3 seconds decide everything: pattern interrupt (unexpected visual, bold claim, question) before your product appears.
Localise: UK English ≠ US English ('checkout' vs 'check out', colour vs color). EU needs translated creatives - don't assume English works.
Test 3-5 creative angles per product: problem-solution, demo, testimonial, offer-led, curiosity.
Broad targeting + good creative often beats hyper-specific interests in 2025 - let Meta's algorithm find buyers.
Lookalikes once you have 100+ customers: 1% lookalike of purchasers is gold.
Exclude past purchasers from prospecting campaigns - they're for retention/upsell campaigns instead.
Geo-targeting: US nationwide or top 10 states by your product's appeal - don't spray globally.

blocks.p: The golden rule: kill campaigns at $100-150 spend with zero purchases, scale winners at 2x ROAS for 5+ days. Everything else is noise.
Member toolkit: the Ad Creative Skill generates the 3-angle test matrix (problem/curiosity/offer) with copy and creative briefs. The SEO Audit Skill finds organic gaps alongside paid. See Products.

title: ASC vs manual campaigns: which structure for your stage
excerpt: Advantage+ Shopping vs manual campaigns - when to use each, how budgets flow, and the structure that scales without chaos.

blocks.p: Campaign structure is where most ad accounts bleed money - too many campaigns fragment learning, too few give Meta no room to optimize.

list: What it is: Meta's AI-driven campaign - you provide products, budget, country; Meta finds buyers automatically.
Best for: new stores, <$5k/month ad spend, when you don't have proven audiences yet.
Pros: simplest setup, leverages Meta's data, good for testing products fast.
Cons: less control over audiences/placements, can overspend on bad placements, harder to scale systematically.
Structure: Campaign (objective) > Ad Set (audience/budget/placements) > Ads (creatives).
Best for: proven products, >$5k/month spend, when you need controlled testing.
Typical structure: 1 campaign per product/angle, 2-3 ad sets (broad, interest, lookalike), 3-5 ads per ad set.
Budget: set at ad set level for control; CBO (campaign budget optimization) once you trust the structure.
One campaign per product or per angle - don't mix winners and losers in one campaign.
Ad set budget $20-50/day minimum - below that, not enough data for Meta to optimize.
Kill fast: ad sets with $100+ spend and zero purchases = dead. Don't wait 'just in case'.
Scale gradually: 20-30% budget increases every 2-3 days on winners - sudden 10x jumps reset learning.
Always keep a testing campaign separate from scaling campaigns - 80% budget on proven, 20% on new tests.

blocks.p: Start with ASC for simplicity; graduate to manual once you have data on what audiences/creatives actually convert for YOUR store.

title: Hooks, creatives & audiences: stop the scroll and find buyers
excerpt: Write hooks that stop thumbs, build creatives that convert, and target audiences without wasting spend.

blocks.p: Your ad has 1.5 seconds to stop a scroll. The hook is everything - creative is the hook + proof + offer, in that order.

list: Pattern interrupt: unexpected visual (before/after, weird product use, bold text overlay).
Curiosity gap: 'This ₹499 gadget replaced my ₹5000 one' - creates open loop.
Relatable pain: 'Still paying ₹2000/month for [problem]?' - speaks to frustration.
Social proof: '10,000+ Indians bought this last month' - numbers create FOMO.
Direct offer: '50% off ends tonight' - works for retargeting, weaker for cold traffic.
UGC-style video (15-30s): phone-shot, authentic, 'I tried this' - highest CTR for ecommerce.
Before/after: transformation results - skincare, home organisation, car accessories.
Demo video: show product working, not just talking about it.
Static images: still work for simple products - clean product shot + benefit text + price.
Carousel: multiple products or angles in one ad - good for collections.
Broad (Advantage+ audience): let Meta find buyers - often best for ecommerce with good creative.
Interest stacking: 3-5 related interests (e.g., 'online shopping' + 'smartphone accessories' + 'mens fashion') - don't stack 20 unrelated ones.
Lookalike 1-3%: once you have 100+ customers, seed from purchasers - highest quality audience.
Retargeting: website visitors (30 days), add-to-cart abandoners (7 days), past purchasers (30 days) - separate campaigns, warmer audiences convert at 3-5x cold.

blocks.p: Testing rule: one variable at a time - new hook OR new audience OR new offer, never all three. Otherwise you don't know what worked.
Member toolkit: the Ad Creative Skill writes hooks, headlines, primary texts and creative briefs for exactly this lesson framework - plus the compliance rules per category. See Products.

title: Metrics, scaling & knowing your real numbers
excerpt: Read ROAS/CPA correctly, scale winners without breaking them, and build the weekly optimisation habit.

blocks.p: Most advertisers look at the wrong metrics and make bad decisions. This lesson is the financial literacy your ad account needs.

list: ROAS (Return on Ad Spend): revenue ÷ ad spend. Break-even = 1 ÷ your margin. 40% margin → need 2.5x just to break even; aim for 3-4x to scale profitably.
CPA (Cost Per Acquisition): ad spend ÷ purchases. Compare against your gross margin per order, not arbitrary benchmarks.
CTR (Click-Through Rate): below 1% = weak creative or wrong audience; above 2% = healthy for cold traffic.
CPC (Cost Per Click): your traffic cost - compare across campaigns, not against 'industry averages'.
Frequency: how many times same person sees your ad. Above 3-4 = ad fatigue, refresh creative.
Gradual increases: 20-30% every 2-3 days on campaigns with consistent 3x+ ROAS - sudden jumps reset learning.
Duplicate before scaling: copy winning campaign, increase budget - keeps original stable while testing higher spend.
Vertical scaling: increase budget on same audience/creative until frequency hits 3+, then horizontal scale (new audiences, new creatives).
Kill losers fast: $100-150 spend with zero purchases = dead. Don't 'give it more time' - that's hope not strategy.
Monday: review last week's ROAS/CPA per campaign - kill underperformers, note winners.
Wednesday: check frequency - above 3 = refresh creative on that ad set.
Friday: scale winners 20%, launch 1-2 new creative tests for next week.
Monthly: review total spend vs revenue - are you actually profitable after product costs and fees?

blocks.p: The brutal truth: 80% of ad tests fail. The skill isn't picking winners upfront - it's killing losers fast and doubling down on what works. That's the whole game.
